subject: Critical Thinking
title: Modus Ponens: The King of Deduction
description: A short lesson to help you apply Modus Ponens: The King of Deduction.

hook.text: If it rains, the street gets wet. It's raining. Therefore the street is wet. Flawless logic — every time.

buildup.text: This pattern is modus ponens: If P then Q. P is true. Therefore Q is true.

discovery.text: It's the most fundamental rule in all of logic — you can build entire mathematical systems from it.

twist.text: Its evil twin, affirming the consequent, tricks millions: 'The street is wet, so it must have rained.' No!

climax.text: The difference between modus ponens and its twin is the #1 logic error in everyday arguments.

punchline.text: If P then Q. Q happened. That doesn't mean P did.

quiz.question: What error does 'affirming the consequent' commit?
options: Assuming Q proves P in 'if P then Q'

details.summary: Modus ponens is the fundamental deductive rule: if P then Q; P is true; therefore Q is true. It is the simplest and most commonly used valid argument form, forming the backbone of logical reasoning.
details.whyItMatters: Modus ponens is used constantly in science, law, and everyday reasoning, making it the single most important rule of inference to master.
takeaways: If P then Q, plus P, yields Q with certainty
It is the most basic valid deductive form
Affirming the consequent is a common invalid imitation

faq.question: What is a simple everyday example of modus ponens?
faq.answer: If it rains, the ground gets wet. It is raining. Therefore the ground is wet. The conditional and the condition together guarantee the conclusion.

faq.question: What is the most common mistake people make with modus ponens?
faq.answer: Affirming the consequent: seeing the ground is wet and concluding it rained. The ground could be wet for other reasons, so the reverse does not follow.
